questions.stem: Why is soil often treated as a non-renewable resource on human time-scales?
options: It is made only of minerals that are mined from rock
It is destroyed whenever plants grow and take up soil water
It forms far more slowly than it can be lost by erosion
It cannot be formed by any natural process on Earth
questions.explanation: Soil forms by slow weathering of rock and build-up of organic matter, while erosion can remove it in a single storm, so lost soil is not replaced within a human lifetime. Soil does form naturally, but over very long periods.

questions.stem: Which farming practice best maintains soil as a sustainable resource on a cropping farm in a windy, dry district?
options: Leaving paddocks bare and fallow through summer
Retaining crop stubble on paddocks between seasons
Burning crop stubble straight after harvest every year
Cultivating the soil several times before sowing
questions.explanation: Stubble covers the soil surface, protecting it from wind and rain, and adds organic matter. Burning, repeated cultivation and bare fallow all leave soil exposed to erosion.

questions.stem: Rows of trees are planted along the edges of paddocks in a district where wind erosion is common. How do they protect the soil?
options: They reduce wind speed near the ground on their sheltered side
They increase wind speed so that soil is blown off more evenly
They add salt to the soil, which binds the grains together firmly
They raise the water table, which keeps the surface soil wetter
questions.explanation: Windbreaks slow the wind for a distance downwind of the trees, so less soil is lifted and carried. Trees use water and tend to lower, not raise, the water table.

questions.stem: Dryland salinity affects farmland across a region. Which explanation links land use to the problem at a regional scale?
options: Heavy rain on cleared land dissolves salt from the air and deposits it in the lowest paddocks
Irrigating with fresh river water dilutes the soil salt so that it spreads into nearby districts
Replacing deep-rooted vegetation with shallow-rooted crops raises saline groundwater across the catchment
Planting deep-rooted trees on hilltops draws salt up from the groundwater into the farm topsoil
questions.explanation: Annual crops and pastures use less water than native vegetation, so more water reaches the water table, which rises and carries stored salt towards the surface in low-lying areas. Deep-rooted trees are a remedy because they lower the water table.

questions.stem: Which is an example of the sustainability of soil being considered at a global scale?
options: Erosion of a single creek bank after cattle trample the edges
Salt scalds forming in the lowest paddock on one family farm
Compaction of a sports oval caused by heavy mowing equipment
Loss of fertile topsoil worldwide threatening future food supply
questions.explanation: The worldwide loss of topsoil affects the ability of the whole planet to grow food, so it is a global issue. The other examples are local changes on one site.

questions.stem: Which situation shows fresh water being used unsustainably?
options: Releasing environmental flows from a dam to a wetland
Recycling treated wastewater to irrigate public parks
Pumping an aquifer faster than rain and rivers recharge it
Collecting rainwater from a house roof in a tank for the garden
questions.explanation: Extracting groundwater faster than it is recharged steadily lowers the stored volume, which cannot continue indefinitely. Rainwater tanks and recycling reduce demand on other sources, and environmental flows protect ecosystems.

questions.stem: Several of the world's major farming regions depend on aquifers whose water tables have fallen steadily for decades. What does this suggest about global food production?
options: Some of it depends on groundwater that is being used faster than it is replaced
All of it depends on surface water, so falling water tables do not affect it
Some of it will increase, because lower water tables make soils easier to farm
None of it is at risk, because aquifers are refilled within a single wet season
questions.explanation: Falling water tables show extraction exceeding recharge, so food grown with that water is not sustainable in the long run. Many large aquifers take decades to millennia to refill.

questions.stem: A town takes water from a river that is also used upstream by irrigators and downstream by a wetland. Why is the sustainability of the town's supply a regional issue rather than only a local one?
options: Rivers are refilled by ocean water, so local use has no effect downstream
Only users in the same town can affect the amount of water in the river
Use anywhere in the catchment changes the water available to every other user
The town's own water use is too small to have any effect on the river flow
questions.explanation: Water in a river is shared through the whole catchment, so extraction upstream reduces flow for the town and use by the town reduces flow for the wetland. Managing it sustainably needs catchment-wide planning.

questions.stem: The Great Artesian Basin underlies about one-fifth of Australia. What type of groundwater system is it?
options: A system of confined aquifers in sandstone layers between impermeable rock
A single shallow unconfined aquifer of sand lying just beneath the surface
A system of underground rivers flowing through large caves in limestone
A large freshwater lake trapped in a cavern beneath the inland deserts
questions.explanation: The basin's water is held in porous sandstone aquifers sandwiched between impermeable layers such as mudstone, which confine it under pressure. It is water held in the pores of rock, not an underground lake or river.

questions.stem: What is the recharge area of an aquifer?
options: Where bores are drilled to pump out the water
Where water enters the aquifer from the surface
Where water leaves the aquifer at a spring
Where the aquifer is deepest below the ground
questions.explanation: The recharge area is where rain or river water soaks down into the aquifer, usually where the aquifer rock is exposed at the surface. Springs and bores are discharge points, where water leaves the aquifer.

questions.stem: Where is the Great Artesian Basin mainly recharged?
options: Across its western edge, where sea water seeps into the rocks from the Indian Ocean
Through the floor of Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, where floodwater drains into the rock
Through bores drilled by landholders, which carry rain directly down into the basin
Along its eastern edge, where its sandstones are exposed near the Great Dividing Range
questions.explanation: Rain and river water soak into the aquifer sandstones where they reach the surface along the eastern margin of the basin. Lake Eyre is near the basin's discharge end, and bores remove water rather than adding it.

questions.stem: Water flows out of many Great Artesian Basin bores without being pumped. What causes this?
options: The weight of the atmosphere is lower in the inland, so water rises up the bore
The recharge area is higher than the bores, so the confined water is under pressure
Heat from the deep rock boils the water, and the steam pushes it up the bore
Plant roots near the bores draw the water upwards and release it at the surface
questions.explanation: Water entering the aquifer at high elevation in the east is confined beneath impermeable layers, so it is under pressure further west and rises up a bore to the surface. This is what makes the water artesian.

questions.stem: Dating shows that water in the central parts of the Great Artesian Basin is more than a million years old, while water near the recharge area is young. What does this show?
options: Water moves very slowly through the basin from recharge to discharge areas
Water enters the basin from the centre and flows outwards towards the edges
Water in the centre was trapped when the rocks formed and is never replaced
Water moves quickly through the basin and is renewed every few years
questions.explanation: The age increases with distance from the recharge area, showing that water takes a very long time to travel through the sandstone. That slow flow is why recovery from overuse is slow.

questions.stem: For about a century, many Great Artesian Basin bores flowed uncontrolled into open earth drains. Why did this waste most of the water?
options: Most of it was taken up by native trees along the bores
Most of it evaporated or seeped away before it was used
Most of it flowed back down into the aquifer it came from
Most of it froze in the drains during cold inland nights
questions.explanation: Open drains run for long distances across hot, dry country, so most of the water was lost to evaporation and seepage rather than reaching stock. Replacing drains with pipes and tanks greatly reduces these losses.

questions.stem: Mound springs in the far north of South Australia are natural outlets of the Great Artesian Basin and support unique plants and animals. Why have some springs weakened or stopped flowing?
options: Extraction from bores has lowered the pressure in the aquifer
Rainfall at the springs has increased, flooding the outlets
The springs were capped as part of state bore-control programs
Salt from the sea has blocked the springs from the outside
questions.explanation: Spring flow depends on aquifer pressure, so heavy extraction from bores lowers pressure and reduces flow at the springs. Capping uncontrolled bores is a remedy that helps pressure recover.

questions.stem: Capping and piping uncontrolled bores is expected to restore pressure in parts of the Great Artesian Basin, but only over many decades. Why so slow?
options: The capped bores leak more water than they did before they were capped
Rain in the recharge area has stopped since the bores were first drilled
Pressure in a confined aquifer cannot rise once it has started to fall
Recharge is slow and water moves slowly through the aquifer to refill it
questions.explanation: Recovery depends on recharge and the slow movement of water through the sandstone, so pressure builds back gradually. Pressure can recover; it is the rate that is slow.

questions.stem: An aquifer has lost 600 GL of stored water. After extraction is reduced, recharge exceeds extraction by 4 GL per year. Assuming this continues, about how long will full recovery take?
options: 1.5 years
150 years
60 years
24 years
questions.explanation: Time = deficit / net gain = 600 / 4 = 150 years. The calculation shows how the replenishment time depends on how much extraction is reduced: halving the net gain would double the recovery time.

questions.stem: Two plans are proposed for an overused groundwater basin. Plan A cuts extraction slightly; Plan B cuts it greatly. How do they compare in replenishment time?
options: Plan A refills the basin faster, because some extraction speeds up flow
Both refill in the same time, because recharge depends only on rainfall
Neither plan affects the time, because groundwater cannot be replenished
Plan B gives a larger net recharge, so the basin refills in less time
questions.explanation: Recovery time is the deficit divided by the net surplus of recharge over extraction, so the bigger the cut, the faster the recovery. Recharge does depend on rainfall, but the net change in storage also depends on extraction.

questions.stem: Why does a city produce much more stormwater run-off than the same area of natural bushland?
options: Cities receive much more rainfall than the surrounding bushland
Buildings release water vapour that condenses into extra rain
Parks and gardens in cities absorb less water than bare rock
Roofs, roads and paving stop rain from soaking into the ground
questions.explanation: Impervious surfaces prevent infiltration, so a far greater share of rain runs off quickly into drains. The rainfall itself is about the same.

questions.stem: Untreated urban stormwater flows through drains into the sea. Which pollutants does it commonly carry?
options: Mainly radioactive dust from the soil beneath the paved streets
Sediment, nutrients, litter, oils and heavy metals from streets
Only rainwater, because drains are separate from sewage pipes
Mainly sea salt, which is washed from the air by rain over the city
questions.explanation: Stormwater picks up sediment, fertiliser, litter, oil and metals such as zinc and copper from roads, roofs and gardens. Being separate from sewage does not make it clean.

questions.stem: In parts of northern Adelaide, stormwater is directed into constructed wetlands before being used. What is the main role of the wetlands?
options: To clean the water as sediment settles and plants take up nutrients
To heat the water so that it can be piped to houses for bathing
To add salt to the water so that it matches the nearby sea water
To evaporate the water so that drains do not overflow in storms
questions.explanation: Slow flow through reeds lets sediment and attached pollutants settle, while plants and microbes remove nutrients and sunlight helps kill pathogens. The cleaned water can then be stored and reused.

questions.stem: After treatment in wetlands, stormwater is injected through bores into an aquifer in winter and pumped out in summer to water parks. What is this process called?
options: Artesian pressure release
Aquifer storage and recovery
Groundwater overextraction control
Seawater intrusion control
questions.explanation: Aquifer storage and recovery is a form of managed aquifer recharge: water is stored underground when it is plentiful and recovered when it is needed. Storing it underground avoids evaporation losses from open storages.

questions.stem: A council compares sending stormwater straight to the sea with harvesting it through wetlands and aquifer storage. Which pair of benefits does harvesting provide?
options: Saltier groundwater in the aquifer and less water available for parks
Less pollution reaching coastal waters and less demand on mains water
More sediment reaching seagrass beds and higher sea levels at the coast
Higher flood peaks in creeks and more water lost to evaporation in summer
questions.explanation: Harvesting keeps polluted run-off out of the sea, protecting seagrass and coastal water quality, and supplies water that would otherwise come from mains. Wetlands also hold back flood peaks.

questions.stem: Why must stormwater be treated before it is injected into an aquifer for storage?
options: Untreated stormwater is too salty to enter a freshwater aquifer at all
Untreated stormwater is too warm, so it would boil when underground
Untreated stormwater is too clean and would dissolve the aquifer rock
Suspended sediment and pollutants can clog the aquifer and degrade its water
questions.explanation: Fine sediment and organic matter block the pores around the injection bore, and contaminants would spoil the stored water for later use. Treatment protects both the aquifer and the quality of the recovered water.

questions.stem: In a coastal aquifer, fresh groundwater floats above denser sea water. What happens to the boundary between them when too much fresh water is pumped out?
options: It moves inland and upwards towards the bores
It moves seaward and downwards away from the bores
It stays fixed, because sea water cannot enter rock
It disappears, because the two waters mix completely
questions.explanation: Pumping lowers the fresh water table and the pressure it exerts, so the denser sea water advances inland and rises beneath the bores. Eventually the bores may draw salty water.

questions.stem: In a coastal aquifer, the fresh-salt boundary lies about 40 m below sea level for every 1 m that the fresh water table stands above sea level. Pumping lowers the water table near a bore from 1.5 m to 1.0 m above sea level. About how far does the boundary rise?
questions.explanation: Depth to the boundary falls from 1.5 x 40 = 60 m to 1.0 x 40 = 40 m, a rise of 20 m. A small drop in the water table therefore causes a large rise in the salt water beneath.

questions.stem: Why does a small fall in the water table of a coastal aquifer cause a large rise in the salt water beneath it?
options: Sea water is much less dense than fresh water
Fresh water is pulled down by the weight of the air
Fresh water is heavier, so it sinks below sea water
Sea water is only slightly denser than fresh water
questions.explanation: Because the density difference is small, a thick lens of fresh water is needed to balance the sea water, so each metre of water table above sea level supports tens of metres of fresh water below. Fresh water is less dense and floats on top.

questions.stem: Which management step would best reduce seawater intrusion into a coastal aquifer used for irrigation?
options: Reducing pumping and recharging the aquifer with treated water
Drilling the irrigation bores deeper to reach more of the water
Moving the irrigation bores closer to the coast to spread pumping
Pumping harder in summer so that the bores are flushed of salt
questions.explanation: Less pumping and artificial recharge raise the fresh water table, pushing the boundary back seaward. Deeper bores or bores nearer the coast would draw in salt water sooner.

questions.stem: Which rural activity is a common source of nitrate pollution in groundwater?
options: Spreading excess nitrogen fertiliser on crops
Planting deep-rooted native trees on hillsides
Building fences to keep stock out of creeks
Leaving crop stubble on paddocks after harvest
questions.explanation: Nitrate is very soluble, so nitrogen not taken up by crops leaches down through the soil to the water table. Trees, fencing and stubble reduce pollution and erosion rather than causing them.

questions.stem: Petrol is found in groundwater beneath a suburb. Which source is most likely?
options: Salt carried inland from the coast by sea breezes
Rain falling on the roofs of houses in the suburb
A leaking underground fuel tank at a service station
Fertiliser spread on lawns and gardens in the surrounding area
questions.explanation: Corroded or damaged underground tanks are a common urban source of hydrocarbons in groundwater. Fertiliser adds nitrate and phosphate, not petrol.

questions.stem: Which industrial activity is most likely to pollute groundwater with acid and dissolved metals?
options: Cooling water released from a wind turbine factory
Rainwater collected from the roof of a warehouse
Steam released from the tall stack of a gas power plant
Drainage from mine waste containing sulfide minerals
questions.explanation: Sulfide minerals such as pyrite in mine waste react with air and water to form sulfuric acid, which dissolves metals that can seep into groundwater. Roof water and steam do not carry acid and metals in this way.

questions.stem: Septic tanks are common in a town on sandy soil with a shallow water table, and nearby household bores show rising nitrate and bacteria. Why is this setting especially vulnerable?
options: Deep water tables give wastewater too long to break down, so it concentrates underground
Sand reacts with the wastewater, which converts harmless compounds into nitrate and bacteria
Wastewater passes quickly through sand with little filtering before reaching the water table
Clay in sandy soil traps the wastewater, which then evaporates into the air above the town
questions.explanation: Coarse sand drains fast and filters poorly, and a shallow water table leaves little unsaturated soil to remove contaminants, so septic effluent reaches the groundwater. Clay soils and deep water tables give more protection.

questions.stem: Why is polluted groundwater generally harder to clean up than a polluted river?
options: It moves quickly and is diluted by rain, so pollutants spread across a whole state
It is exposed to sunlight, which breaks pollutants into more toxic compounds
It contains no microorganisms at all, so nothing can be done to treat it
It moves slowly and is hidden underground, so pollutants persist and are hard to reach
questions.explanation: Groundwater flows slowly through pores, so pollutants stay for years to decades, and they can only be reached through bores. A river flushes contaminants downstream far more quickly.

questions.stem: A monitoring bore downhill from an old landfill shows rising ammonia and dissolved salts. What is the most likely cause?
options: Leachate from rotting waste seeping down into the groundwater
Sea water entering the aquifer as rainfall over the landfill
Nitrogen gas from the air dissolving in rain over the bore
Methane from the landfill condensing as water inside the bore
questions.explanation: Rain percolating through decomposing waste forms leachate rich in ammonia, salts and other contaminants, which can enter groundwater if the landfill is unlined. This is why modern landfills have liners and leachate collection.

questions.stem: Which source of water for a city does not depend on rainfall?
options: A dam on a local river
A rainwater tank system
Desalinated sea water
Harvested stormwater
questions.explanation: Desalination takes water from the sea, so it keeps supplying water through droughts. Stormwater, river dams and rainwater tanks all rely on rain falling in the catchment.

questions.stem: Adelaide has a seawater desalination plant that can supply water in droughts. Which is a main limitation of desalination?
options: It adds salt to the water supply, making it unsafe for drinking
It draws water from rivers, reducing environmental flows inland
It uses large amounts of energy and produces concentrated brine
It can only operate when rainfall over the city is above average
questions.explanation: Reverse osmosis needs large amounts of electricity to push sea water through membranes, and the concentrated brine returned to the sea must be dispersed to avoid harming marine life. Its benefit is a supply independent of rainfall.

questions.stem: A city weighs three ways to add to its water supply: a desalination plant, stormwater harvesting and a new dam on a river. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Desalination is reliable in drought but costly in energy; stormwater harvesting uses a wasted resource but depends on rain
Desalination depends on rain but uses no energy; stormwater harvesting is reliable in drought but adds pollution to the sea
A new dam has no environmental effects and is reliable in drought; desalination has no effect on the marine environment
Stormwater harvesting needs sea water to operate; desalination and a new dam both depend only on groundwater supplies
questions.explanation: Desalination is independent of rainfall but energy-hungry and produces brine; stormwater harvesting turns a pollutant into a resource but yields little in dry years. A dam changes river flows and holds little in drought.
